items.narration_anchor: De los hombres que habían pasado por la mina, cincuenta y nueve de cada cien se habían ido antes de cumplir seis meses.

items.subject: a Spanish migrant couple, a stocky man in his early 30s in a worn dark overcoat and a slight woman in her late 20s in a wool coat and headscarf, with a small boy of about four clutching her coat hem, seen from behind climbing a stairwell with suitcases

items.subject: a Spanish migrant family, a broad-shouldered man in his 30s in a short-sleeve shirt and a woman in her early 30s in a sun-faded cotton dress, seen from behind loading suitcases into a dusty 1960s sedan outside their Wittenoom house

items.narration_anchor: Los de Juan-Barroso estuvieron unos dos años y medio en el pueblo y volvieron a Madrid en mil novecientos setenta y uno; Mercedes de Juan se quedó en Australia.

items.subject: the town of Wittenoom seen from above, its grid of streets and scattered iron-roofed houses, a wind-driven veil of blue-grey dust rolling through the empty main street

items.narration_anchor: Cerró la mina. Nadie cerró el polvo. Veinte años después, un policía iba a reconocer el nombre del pueblo en un pasaporte.

items.narration_anchor: Mil novecientos ochenta y cinco. Un aeropuerto australiano, un puesto de control. El agente abre el documento de Daniel Écija hijo, lee el lugar de nacimiento, baja la cabeza hacia el papel, vuelve a mirarlo.

items.subject: an open passport lying flat on the beige laminate checkpoint counter, the typed place-of-birth line catching the light

text_in_image.location: place-of-birth line of the open passport page

items.narration_anchor: «Así que de Wittenoom, ¿eh? Un sitio terrorífico», dijo el policía.

items.subject: the town of Wittenoom at its entrance road, a government warning sign planted at the roadside, boarded houses and a flatbed truck lashed with furniture beyond

text_in_image.location: roadside warning sign at the town entrance

items.narration_anchor: Para entonces, desde mil novecientos setenta y ocho, el gobierno del Estado venía reduciendo el pueblo y empujando a la gente a irse, por las fibras en el aire.

items.subject: a weathered yellow bulldozer pushing through a corrugated iron and asbestos cement house, the structure folding into a plume of dust

items.mood: a house folding into dust under hard light, bare slabs where the neighbours stood, the cab lost in the plume
items.narration_anchor: Entre mil novecientos ochenta y seis y mil novecientos noventa y dos demolieron edificios y cerraron los servicios básicos.

items.subject: the abandoned Wittenoom airstrip, a long flat strip surfaced with blue-grey asbestos tailings cutting across the red plain, a torn windsock hanging limp

items.narration_anchor: En mil novecientos noventa y tres cerró el aeropuerto. Seis años después de aquel control, su padre fue al médico.

items.subject: a Spanish man in his mid-50s, stocky, greying dark hair, lined work-worn face, in a wool jacket and open collar, seated in profile in a consulting room beside a glowing X-ray light box
items.action: he sits waiting for the doctor's words, the chest X-ray clipped on the light box beside him, his body sunk back into the chair

items.mood: a man sunk into a chair under cold light, the glowing radiograph beside him, a closed door he keeps looking at
items.narration_anchor: Madrid, mil novecientos noventa y uno. Daniel Écija va al médico. Le hacen pruebas. La palabra es mesotelioma. Nueve meses.

items.subject: a sepia baptism photograph from 1963, a young Spanish migrant couple with an infant outside an iron-roofed house, propped on a bedroom dresser in a Madrid flat

items.narration_anchor: Daniel muere a los cincuenta y cinco años, veintiocho años después de la foto del bautizo.

items.gaze_interaction: her face turned down toward the bandaged-foot photograph, shoulders curved inward, body tilted toward the table as if closing around it

items.narration_anchor: Décadas más tarde, María está en una habitación rodeada de fotografías en sepia. Entre ellas, la del pie vendado. «Me pegué a mi marido, como una niña pequeña», dice la viuda.

items.subject: the elderly Spanish widow in her mid-80s, slight build, white hair pinned back, dark cardigan, seen from behind and in profile, head bowed over the table of sepia photographs
items.action: she bows her head toward the small bandaged-foot photograph on the table before her, her shoulders drawn inward and her back curved under the window light

items.mood: a bowed white head and curved shoulders rimmed by hard light, the room dark behind, sepia faces blurred on the table
items.narration_anchor: Uno de los hijos dice que ese sitio les cambió la vida para siempre. Daniel no fue el primero. Para entonces, el Estado ya tenía un número.
